findings.claim: Image created with Google Gemini Pro
findings.issue: By 2026, Google's dedicated image-generation models under Gemini are branded as 'Gemini Pro Image' / 'Nano Banana Pro' rather than plain 'Google Gemini Pro' (which primarily denotes the text reasoning tier). The attribution is close enough not to mislead a beginner audience, but 'Gemini' or 'Gemini Pro Image' would be more precise. Non-blocking.

findings.claim: Local models are typically smaller and less capable than the frontier cloud models.
findings.issue: Still broadly accurate as of 2026, with the minor caveat that Ollama now also offers an optional paid cloud tier for larger datacenter-hosted models. The core claim comparing locally-runnable models to frontier cloud models remains correct and the nuance does not affect a beginner explanation.

newData.body:
A curated collection of the best places to learn more about AI, large language models, and the broader landscape. ### **Foundational Reading**

Attention Is All You Need — Original Transformer Paper

The 2017 Google research paper that introduced the Transformer architecture which underpins every modern LLM.

AcademicArchitecture

arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 ↗

The Illustrated Transformer — Jay Alammar

The clearest visual explanation of how transformers work. Essential reading for anyone wanting to understand the mechanics without heavy maths.

VisualBeginner-friendly

jalammar.github.io ↗

Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3 Paper)

OpenAI's landmark 2020 paper introducing GPT-3 and the concept of few-shot learning at scale.

AcademicOpenAI

arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165 ↗
### **Courses & Interactive Learning**

fast.ai — Practical Deep Learning for Coders

Free, hands-on course that takes you from basics to building real neural networks. No heavy maths prerequisites.

FreeCoursePractical

course.fast.ai ↗

Andrej Karpathy — Neural Networks: Zero to Hero

YouTube series by former Tesla and OpenAI researcher. Builds a neural network from scratch in Python. One of the best free resources available.

FreeYouTubeCoding

YouTube Playlist ↗

DeepLearning.AI Short Courses

Short courses on LLMs, prompt engineering, RAG, and agents, taught by Andrew Ng and leading practitioners from partner labs and companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta. Each typically runs about one to two hours. As of 2026-10-03, the large catalogue of short courses is mostly free to access — the gate is an email address, not a credit card — and DeepLearning.AI also offers a paid Pro subscription that unlocks some newer content and extras. Pricing and what sits behind the paywall change over time, so check the course page for the current terms. Ideal for non-technical learners who want to start watching and experimenting quickly.

Mostly freeCourseBeginner-friendly

deeplearning.ai/courses ↗
### **News & Commentary**

The Batch — DeepLearning.AI Newsletter

Weekly AI news and commentary from DeepLearning.AI, with a personal letter from Andrew Ng in every issue. It focuses on the realities of AI — what's actually happening and what it means — so readers can keep up without being misled by hype. Clear, balanced, and accessible for non-technical readers.

NewsletterWeekly

deeplearning.ai/the-batch ↗

Import AI — Jack Clark

Detailed weekly newsletter from Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic and, as of 2026-10-03, the company's Head of Public Benefit, where he leads the Anthropic Institute (the in-house research effort announced in March 2026). He previously served as Anthropic's Head of Policy. Covers research, policy, and the strategic AI landscape, and has well over 100,000 subscribers. Read it on his own site, which is the canonical home for the archive.

NewsletterResearch

jack-clark.net ↗

Simon Willison's Blog

Practical, technically sharp commentary on LLM developments — how they actually work, what they are good at, and where they fail. Written by an independent researcher and open-source maintainer.

BlogTechnical

simonwillison.net ↗
### **Model Playgrounds**

Ollama — Run models locally

Download and run open-weight models on your own computer. Free, private, no API costs.

FreeLocalOpen source

ollama.com ↗

Hugging Face — Model Hub

The GitHub of AI models. Browse, download, and test thousands of open models. Essential reference for the open AI ecosystem.

FreeModelsCommunity

huggingface.co ↗
newData.title: Interesting Resources

findings.claim: OpenAI's current flagship family is GPT-5.6, which was released publicly on July 9, 2026 ... as three models: Sol ... Terra ... and Luna.
findings.issue: Stale state-of-the-world presented as current — the pipeline's primary failure mode. GPT-5.6 is no longer OpenAI's flagship. OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra on September 3, 2026 as its new flagship, with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna following on September 22, 2026. As of the current date (2026-10-03), GPT-6 Astra is the flagship and GPT-5.6 is a superseded generation. The model-card title/lineup and the word 'current' must be rewritten to reflect GPT-6 Astra as flagship, with GPT-5.6 reframed historically (e.g., 'released July 2026, now succeeded by GPT-6').

findings.claim: In practice, eligible paid plans access GPT-5.6 Sol through ChatGPT's reasoning settings while GPT-5.5 Instant remains the default for everyday chat.
findings.issue: Presents a superseded product state as current. Following the GPT-6 Astra launch (Sept 3, 2026), ChatGPT's engine is now GPT-6 Astra (GPT-6 Pro in chat on Pro/Business/Enterprise). The claim that GPT-5.6 Sol is reached via reasoning settings and GPT-5.5 Instant is the everyday default was accurate in July–August 2026 but is no longer the current state. Must be reframed historically or updated.

findings.claim: a 1 million token context window
findings.issue: Imprecise/understated. The documented context window for all three GPT-5.6 models is 1,050,000 tokens (commonly cited as 1.05M), not 1 million. The 128,000 maximum output tokens figure is correct.

findings.claim: a February 2026 knowledge cutoff
findings.issue: Imprecise but not wrong. The documented knowledge cutoff is specifically February 16, 2026. 'February 2026' is an acceptable rounding but could be made exact.

findings.claim: models: 'Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5'; description presents this as the current lineup
findings.issue: This lineup is stale as of today (2026-10-03). The current lineup is Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 (latest, released Sept 28, 2026), with Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, and restricted-access Mythos 5.1 also active. Opus 4.8 was superseded by Opus 5 (July 24, 2026) and then Opus 5.5; it is now a previous/legacy generation. Fable 5 was superseded by Fable 5.1 on Sept 1, 2026. Presenting Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 as the current tier is exactly the pipeline's known failure mode and must be corrected or re-framed historically before publication.

findings.claim: As of July 21, 2026, Claude Fable 5 is available globally ... Anthropic describes it as its most capable widely released model, sitting above the Opus tier.
findings.issue: The 'as of July 21, 2026' anchor presents a ~2.5-month-old snapshot as the site's current state. While Fable 5 was accurately Anthropic's 'most capable widely released model' at that time, that title now belongs to Fable 5.1 (released Sept 1, 2026). Published today without historical framing, this misrepresents the current state of the world. The date itself is also unverified — the documented availability milestones are June 9 (launch), June 12 (suspension), June 30 (controls lifted), July 1 (access restored); July 21 does not correspond to a known Fable 5 milestone.

findings.claim: US export controls imposed on June 12 were lifted on June 30 and access was restored on July 1
findings.issue: This chronology is accurate: controls imposed June 12, 2026; lifted by Commerce June 30; global access restored July 1. No correction needed, included for completeness.

findings.claim: context window of up to 1 million tokens on its Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 models at flat per-token pricing (Haiku 4.5 supports 200,000 tokens)
findings.issue: Context window figures are correct (Opus/Sonnet 5 = 1M, Haiku 4.5 = 200K). The phrase 'flat per-token pricing' is questionable: Anthropic's long-context (>200K) usage has historically carried premium long-context pricing tiers rather than a single flat rate, so 'flat' may be inaccurate. Worth verifying against the current pricing page before publication.

findings.claim: The current Gemini lineup is 'Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite,' with Gemini 3.5 Flash presented as the current fast/efficient model.
findings.issue: This is a superseded lineup presented as current — the exact failure mode flagged. Gemini 3.5 Flash was released at Google I/O on May 19, 2026 and has since been superseded four times in the Flash line: Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite (GA July 21, 2026), 3.7 Flash (Aug 13, 2026), and 3.8 Flash (GA Sept 2, 2026). As of today (2026-10-03), the current generally available Flash model is Gemini 3.8 Flash. The draft should either be updated to the current lineup or reframed historically.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.5 Flash ... scoring 55 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index while running faster than most models in its intelligence tier.
findings.issue: The '55' figure was accurate for Gemini 3.5 Flash (high reasoning) at its May 2026 launch, but it is attached to a stale model presented as current. The current Flash model, Gemini 3.8 Flash, scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (high reasoning). Presenting the 55 figure as the current state is blocking because it misrepresents the present lineup.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite is part of the named lineup.
findings.issue: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (preview March 3, 2026; GA May 8, 2026) was itself superseded by Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite (GA July 21, 2026). If the lineup is updated, the Flash-Lite entry should be refreshed to 3.5 Flash-Lite.

findings.claim: Gemini 3.5 Flash offers a 1 million–token context window.
findings.issue: This specific claim is accurate (the current 3.8 Flash also has a 1M-token context window), so it survives even an update to the lineup. Noted only for completeness.

findings.claim: The draft contains no explicit 'as of <date>' statement.
findings.issue: The description makes present-tense currency claims (e.g., 'is a strong pick', 'running faster than most models in its intelligence tier') without any dated 'as of' anchor. Per the house rule, currency claims about a fast-moving model lineup should carry an explicit date; its absence here compounds the stale-lineup problem and the content should not be published present-tense without a date.

findings.claim: Grok 4.5 as the current flagship since its July 8, 2026 release
findings.issue: Grok 4.5 is no longer the current flagship — it has been superseded twice. Grok 4.6 shipped August 12, 2026, and Grok 4.7 (released September 21, 2026) is xAI's current flagship as of today (2026-10-03). The July 8, 2026 release date for Grok 4.5 is itself accurate, but presenting Grok 4.5 as 'the current flagship' presents a stale state of the world as current. Current correct flagship: Grok 4.7.

findings.claim: models: Grok 4.5 · Grok 4.3 · Grok 4.1 Fast (presented as the current lineup)
findings.issue: The current lineup is misrepresented. The flagship should be Grok 4.7 (with Grok 4.6 and 4.5 below it), not Grok 4.5. Additionally, Grok 4.1 Fast was retired from the API on May 15, 2026, so listing it as a current budget tier is stale. The current active lineup centers on Grok 4.7/4.6/4.5 (500K), Grok 4.3/4.20 (1M), and Grok Build 0.1.

findings.claim: Grok 4.1 Fast, a budget, high-throughput option with a 2M-token window
findings.issue: Grok 4.1 Fast was retired from the xAI API on May 15, 2026 and is no longer an available option. (The 2M-token window figure matched it while it existed, but it is presented as currently available, which is stale.)

findings.claim: Grok 4.3, the lower-cost 1M-context tier launched in April 2026
findings.issue: Date is roughly correct (Grok 4.3 launched approximately April 17, 2026) and the 1M context window is accurate. The concern is only that Grok 4.3 is no longer the second tier below the true flagship; in the corrected lineup it sits as a cheaper 1M general-purpose model below the 4.5/4.6/4.7 flagship tier.

findings.claim: Grok 4.5 ... priced at $2 per million input tokens and $6 per million output ... 500K-token context window
findings.issue: These specific figures for Grok 4.5 are accurate ($2/$6 per million input/output, 500K context). No correction needed to the numbers themselves; flagged only because they are attached to a model wrongly labeled as current.

findings.claim: Meta's Llama 4 family remains the most widely deployed open-weight AI ecosystem... Llama 3.3 70B remains a widely-deployed practical text-only option.
findings.issue: These are present-tense 'state of the world' claims with NO explicit date anchor anywhere in the content. House rule requires an explicit 'as of <date>'. Bare present-tense currency claims without a date are a blocking finding. Add an explicit date (e.g., 'as of October 2026') or reframe historically.

findings.claim: In April 2026, Meta Superintelligence Labs launched a new proprietary model, Muse Spark, as the engine behind Meta AI — a strategic pivot away from Llama as Meta's frontier effort.
findings.issue: This presents the April 2026 launch state as the current situation. The Muse lineup has advanced substantially since: Muse Spark 1.1 (July 9, 2026), Muse Spark 1.2 (Aug 5-6, 2026), and the current flagship Muse Spark 1.3 (Sept 2, 2026). Describing plain 'Muse Spark' as the present engine is stale. The current proprietary flagship is Muse Spark 1.3.

findings.claim: a strategic pivot away from Llama as Meta's frontier effort, though existing Llama models remain open and available for self-hosting.
findings.issue: The 'pivot away from open weights' framing is now outdated and presented as the current state. On August 10, 2026, Meta released Muse Glimmer, a ~30B open-weight model under Apache 2.0, and committed to open-weighting Muse Spark 1.2 — reversing the closed-only approach. The content omits this material reversal, presenting a superseded strategic narrative as current.

findings.claim: Llama 4 Scout offers ... a 10-million-token context window — the largest of any openly available model.
findings.issue: Factually consistent with Meta's specs (Scout 10M context, Maverick 1M context, both natively multimodal MoE) and the superlative held at Llama 4's launch. However, presented as current without a date; given the expanding open-weight landscape (e.g., Muse Glimmer), the 'largest of any openly available model' superlative should carry a date anchor or historical framing to stay safe.

findings.claim: Model names presented as CURRENT: 'Llama 4 Maverick · Llama 4 Scout · Llama 3.3 70B'.
findings.issue: These models exist and their individual specs are correct, but the card frames the Llama 4 lineup as Meta's current frontier/flagship ecosystem. As of the content's framing, Meta's frontier effort is the proprietary Muse family (current flagship Muse Spark 1.3), and Meta's newest open-weight model is Muse Glimmer (Aug 2026). The Llama models are valid as legacy/self-hostable options but should not be framed as Meta's current frontier.

findings.claim: Muse Spark 1.1 (current); 'As of July 2026, the current model in this family is Muse Spark 1.1'
findings.issue: Presents a superseded lineup as current. The page will auto-publish on 2026-10-03, by which point two newer releases exist: Muse Spark 1.2 (released August 5, 2026) and Muse Spark 1.3 (released September 2, 2026), which is the current/default version with a 1M-token context. The draft omits both 1.2 and 1.3 and labels 1.1 as current. The 'As of July 2026' date is technically present but the content frames a stale state of the world as the present-tense current lineup, which is this pipeline's named failure mode.

findings.claim: models: 'Muse Spark 1.1 (current), Muse Spark 1.0'
findings.issue: There is no 'Muse Spark 1.0'. The original model (introduced April 2026) was called simply 'Muse Spark' with no version number; version numbering began at 1.1. Meta's own 1.1 blog describes it as 'a significant upgrade from Muse Spark', not from a '1.0'. The version list is also incomplete (missing 1.2 and 1.3).

findings.claim: released ... as its second Meta Superintelligence Labs model
findings.issue: Imprecise. Muse Spark 1.1 was the second release in the Muse Spark family, but MSL also ships other models (e.g., Muse Image/Video around the same window). 'Second MSL model' overstates; 'second Muse Spark release' would be accurate.

findings.claim: DeepSeek V4 Pro & DeepSeek V4 Flash — the current model lineup; 'DeepSeek V4 Pro is the current flagship'
findings.issue: This presents a superseded lineup as current. On September 10, 2026 DeepSeek released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (552B-parameter MoE, native multimodal vision, 1M context) and retired the original V4-Flash and its experimental vision model, routing their API identifiers to V4.1-Flash. In addition, from 04:00 UTC on September 14, 2026, deepseek-v4-pro API requests are routed to V4.1-Flash at Flash prices until a (currently unreleased) V4.1-Pro ships. As of today (2026-10-03), 'V4 Flash' is not the current Flash model, and V4 Pro is no longer served as the default flagship. The card should reflect V4.1-Flash and the V4-Pro routing status, ideally with an explicit 'as of' date.

findings.claim: DeepSeek V4 Pro is the current flagship ... Both are available as open weights and via the DeepSeek API.
findings.issue: Missing required explicit 'as of <date>' anchor for a present-tense state-of-the-world claim, and the claim is factually stale: V4 Flash is retired on the API (its name routes to V4.1-Flash) and V4-Pro API traffic is routed to V4.1-Flash as of September 14, 2026. An explicit date is required by house rule and would also make the staleness visible.

findings.claim: DeepSeek's January 2025 release of R1 shocked the AI industry by matching OpenAI o1's reasoning benchmark performance at a fraction of the training cost.
findings.issue: Accurate and correctly historically framed. R1 was released January 2025 and matched o1 across math/coding/reasoning at ~90-95% lower cost. No change needed; included only for completeness.

findings.claim: so "open-weight" is a promise rather than a download ... nobody outside Alibaba can run it yet
findings.issue: Stale state presented as current — the pipeline's signature failure. This was only true at the July 19, 2026 preview. Alibaba actually released the Qwen3.8-Max weights (Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, 2.4T total / 95B active, custom Qwen3.8-Max Licence) around August 12-14, 2026, and the model is runnable via providers such as OpenRouter and Together AI. It is no longer a promise-only, un-runnable model.

findings.claim: which Alibaba claims performs "second only to Fable 5" — though that claim shipped with no benchmark table, no model card, no license, and no active-parameter count
findings.issue: Mixed stale/incorrect. The active-parameter count WAS disclosed at the August 3, 2026 official launch (~95B active per token, ~4% of 2.4T total). The 'no license / no active-parameter count' characterization describes only the July 19 preview state and is presented as the current state of the world.

findings.claim: models: Qwen3.8-Max-Preview, Qwen3.7-Max, Qwen3.7-Plus, Qwen3.6-27B (open weights)
findings.issue: The lineup is framed as current but lists the superseded preview build. Qwen3.8-Max officially launched (GA) on August 3, 2026 — it is no longer 'Preview'. It should be listed as Qwen3.8-Max, and it is itself now available as open weights, contradicting the body text.

findings.claim: if you specifically want to self-host, the genuinely open line is the earlier Qwen3.6 family, which remains a solid free option
findings.issue: Qwen3.6-27B (Apache 2.0, released April 22, 2026) is genuinely open and still usable, but it has been superseded as the default open option by Qwen3.8-27B (Apache 2.0, released ~August 13-14, 2026). Presenting Qwen3.6 as the go-to open line understates the current open lineup.

findings.claim: "second only to Fable 5"
findings.issue: Accurate to Alibaba's own wording, but 'Fable 5' refers specifically to Anthropic's Claude Fable 5; naming it fully avoids ambiguity. Also note this remains a self-reported, unverified claim with no independent benchmark confirmation.

findings.claim: Entire description uses present-tense, time-sensitive claims ('yet', 'current', 'remains') with no explicit 'as of <date>' anchor.
findings.issue: No bare 'as of writing/today' phrase appears, so the blocking date rule is not literally triggered, but the content makes rapidly-changing claims (open-weight availability, flagship status) with no date anchor, which is precisely what let the stale state slip through. An explicit 'as of <date>' should be added.

findings.claim: models: 'Kimi K3 (current flagship), K3 Swarm Max'
findings.issue: Internal naming inconsistency. The standard flagship variant is officially named 'K3 Max' (chat/agent all-rounder), not bare 'Kimi K3'. The description field correctly calls it 'K3 Max for chat and agents,' but the structured models list labels it 'Kimi K3 (current flagship),' which doesn't match the two-variant naming (K3 Max / K3 Swarm Max). Recommend aligning the models field to 'Kimi K3 Max (current flagship), K3 Swarm Max' for consistency.

findings.claim: prior: K2.7 Code, K2.6, K2.5, K2
findings.issue: The prior-model list omits Kimi K2.8 Preview, which Moonshot released September 11, 2026 (after K3's July launch) as a multimodal model positioned between K2.7 Code and the K3 flagship. This does not affect the central claim that K3 is the current flagship, but the lineup is incomplete. Note that K2.8 Preview post-dates K3, so 'prior' framing is debatable; consider noting it separately if lineup completeness matters.

findings.claim: roughly 2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model
findings.issue: 2.8T is the consensus and officially cited figure (104B active, 896 experts, 16 active per token), so the claim is correct. Minor caveat: some early launch-day coverage (e.g., Fortune, July 16) reported 2.7T before the 2.8T figure settled. The draft's 'roughly 2.8-trillion' phrasing is accurate and not a problem.

findings.claim: Mistral Medium 3.5 ... released as open weights
findings.issue: Accurate, but worth noting the specific license is a 'Modified MIT' license, not Apache 2.0 like the other two models. The weights are published on Hugging Face. The draft's generic 'open weights' is correct but could be more precise.

findings.claim: Mistral Medium 3.5 is the newest
findings.issue: Correct within this three-model lineup (Medium 3.5 ~April 28-29, 2026; Small 4 March 16, 2026; Large 3 December 2025). However, Mistral has shipped even newer products in 2026 (e.g., Voxtral TTS in late March 2026 and other releases), so 'newest' is only true relative to the three models listed, not Mistral's entire catalog.

findings.claim: now the default in Mistral's own Vibe and Le Chat tools
findings.issue: Supported: Medium 3.5 replaced Devstral 2 in the Vibe CLI and retired Magistral from Le Chat. Minor nuance — Le Chat was renamed/rebranded toward 'Mistral Vibe' in 2026, so listing both Vibe and Le Chat as separate current tools is slightly imprecise, but both names remain in use in sources and this is not a factual error.

spotAuditFindings.issue: OpenAI shipped the GPT-6 generation (Astra ~Sep 3; Sol and Luna Sep 22, 2026) as direct replacements for the GPT-5.6 line at ~50% lower prices (Sol $2/$10, Luna $0.10/$0.50). The tracker still lists GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and GPT-5.6 Luna, which are now the superseded prior generation. This is a full-family refresh an informed reader would expect to see.

Anthropic released Claude Opus 5.5 (Sep 22) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Sep 28, 2026), both now Anthropic's recommended current models, with Opus 5.5 priced at $4/$20 (down from Opus 5's $5/$25). The tracker still lists Claude Opus 5 and Claude Sonnet 5 as the current entries, missing the .5 refresh of both tiers.
xAI released Grok 4.7 on September 21, 2026 (with Grok 4.6 shipping earlier). The tracker still lists Grok 4.5, now two point releases behind.

A significant AI price war broke out on Sep 22, 2026: OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol/Luna and Anthropic's Opus 5.5 both cut API prices by roughly 40-50% within hours of each other, halving the cost of frontier-tier inference. No existing or recently-completed Trends topic covers this consumer/developer-relevant pricing shift.
